---
title: "Reading TypeScript"
subtitle: "Enough to read the code, and to ignore the types until you want them."
---

*Snail Assassin* is written in **TypeScript**: JavaScript with **types** added. The types say what kind of value each variable, argument and property holds. Before the game runs, Vite strips them all out, and what's left is ordinary JavaScript.

So you can read TypeScript as JavaScript: **skip everything after a colon, up to the next `,`, `)`, `=` or `{`.**

## Annotations

```ts
export function wrap(v: number, size: number): number {
  return ((v % size) + size) % size;
}
```

Read it as `function wrap(v, size) { ... }`. The `: number` after each argument says it must be a number; the one after the `)` says the function returns a number. If you call `wrap('left', 10)`, your editor underlines it in red before you ever run the game.

## Describing an object: `interface`

{{< snippet repo="minus80" file="snail-assassin/src/systems/predator.ts" method="Predator" >}}

An `interface` is a description of an object's shape: which properties it has and what type each one is. It produces no code at all. Wherever a `Predator` is expected, TypeScript checks the object really has a `pos`, a `mode`, and so on.

`Vec2` is another interface defined in the game: `{ x: number; y: number }`.

## A list of allowed values

{{< snippet repo="minus80" file="snail-assassin/src/systems/predator.ts" method="PredatorMode" >}}

A **union** of strings: a `PredatorMode` can only ever be one of those three words. Write `o.mode = 'chasing'` and it's an error, not a bug you find a week later. In *Cold Chain*, `this.facing` is a string that's supposed to be `'down'`, `'up'` or `'side'`; nothing stops a typo. This is the kind of mistake types catch.

## Classes with types

{{< snippet repo="minus80" file="snail-assassin/src/scenes/HuntScene.ts" lines="36-62" >}}

Mostly familiar from [lesson 1](../lessons/01-javascript.qmd#classes), with additions:

- `private state!: HuntState;` declares a property that will be set later (in `create`), and says what type it holds.
- `private` means only this class may use it.
- `readonly` means it's set once and never changed.
- `!` after a name means "trust me, this will be set before it's used".
- `TouchControls | null` means "a `TouchControls`, or `null`": the `|` reads as *or*.
- `new Map<number, Phaser.GameObjects.Image>()` is a `Map` from numbers to images. The angle brackets give the types of its keys and values.
- `override update(...)` replaces a method `Phaser.Scene` already has.

*Cold Chain* declares its properties by assigning them in `create()`. TypeScript wants them listed at the top of the class, with their types, which doubles as a list of everything the scene keeps track of.

## Imports of types

```ts
import type { CharacterConfig } from '../characters/types';
```

`import type` brings in only a type, for checking. It disappears completely from the built game.

## A constant that stays exact

```ts
export const PALETTE = {
  navy: 0x06192b,
  // ...
} as const;
```

`as const` tells TypeScript the object will never change, so it can treat every value as exact. You can read it as "this is a fixed table".

## Why bother?

Look back at the bugs in this course's exercises: a misspelt texture key ([2.3](../lessons/02-first-scene.qmd#exercises)), `this` in the wrong place ([1.4](../lessons/01-javascript.qmd#exercises)), a missing `true` ([5.3](../lessons/05-assets.qmd#exercises)). Types don't catch all of them, but they catch a lot of that family, in the editor, as you type. In a 600-line game that's a convenience. In a 4,500-line one, it's what keeps the code changeable.

You don't have to use TypeScript for your capstone. But a Vite project can switch at any time: rename `main.js` to `main.ts`, and start adding types where they help.

## Find it in the code

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise F1.1: Read it as JavaScript" .exercise #ex-f1.1}
Rewrite this method from `HuntScene.ts` as plain JavaScript, the way it would look in *Cold Chain*:

```ts
private pauseHunt(): void {
  if (this.ended) return;
  this.scene.launch('Pause', { characterId: this.character.id });
  this.scene.pause();
}
```
